rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: UKHSA guidance covers norovirus outbreak management in hospitals and community health and social care settings.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: Norovirus commonly causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea and spreads readily in close-contact settings.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: People with symptoms should stay away from work, school or nursery until 48 hours after symptoms stop.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: Hands should be washed thoroughly with soap and warm water because alcohol hand gels do not kill norovirus.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: Bleach-based disinfectants are recommended for contaminated surfaces.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: Contaminated clothing and bedding should be washed with detergent at 60 degrees Celsius where possible.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: People who are ill should avoid preparing food for others until 48 hours after symptoms stop.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: UKHSA surveillance combines laboratory, hospital-outbreak and molecular data to monitor activity and variants.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: Norovirus risk depends on setting, contact patterns, surface contamination, hygiene, outbreak status, age, immunity and timing.

rows.source: UKHSA norovirus prevention and outbreak management
rows.verified: UKHSA norovirus evidence is outbreak-, setting-, person-, genotype-, surveillance- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: UKHSA publishes guidance for managing close community contacts of invasive group A streptococcal cases.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: The community-contact guidance applies to confirmed and probable invasive GAS cases.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: Risk assessment and public-health action are linked to defined exposure periods and close-contact criteria.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: The guidance includes algorithms for managing contacts and deciding on prophylaxis.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: UKHSA guidance includes specific considerations for nurseries, schools and other childcare settings.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: Invasive GAS cases are confirmed through laboratory testing of specimens from normally sterile sites.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: UKHSA monitors invasive GAS activity through national surveillance and publishes updated data.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: Secure-setting guidance assigns coordinated prevention and management actions to healthcare, custodial and health-protection teams.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: Invasive-GAS risk depends on strain, clinical syndrome, contact intensity, setting, host factors, wound status and response timing.

rows.source: UKHSA invasive group A streptococcal disease management
rows.verified: UKHSA iGAS evidence is case-, contact-, setting-, organism-, intervention- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
